AST SpaceMobile × Rakuten: the Japan J-LEO Constellation Deal

  • Direct-to-Device
  • Deal Analysis
  • Japan
  • Government

An analysis of the J-LEO grant of up to ¥148bn (~$1B) to RAST, the Rakuten–AST joint venture. It finds the figure is a government grant ceiling, not a purchase price; there is no official satellite count (the 136-satellite J-BLUEBIRD ITU filing is the closest indicator); and the programme carries Japan-based control requirements.

AST SpaceMobile × Rakuten: the Japan “J-LEO” Constellation Deal

What was agreed, what the ~$1B really is, how many satellites Japan gets, and who controls them

Research note • Status as of 28 October 2026 (America/Los_Angeles) • Sources: SEC filings, Japanese government (MIC/CIAJ) documents, Rakuten disclosures, earnings-call transcript and reputable press. Inline numbers in square brackets are clickable and map to the numbered reference list at the end.

1. Executive summary

Bottom line: There is no announced ~$1B purchase of satellites by Rakuten from AST. The “~$1B” is the Japanese government subsidy ceiling for MIC’s J-LEO programme. A Rakuten–AST joint venture, RAST Co., Ltd. (applicant), together with Rakuten Mobile (joint proposer), was selected for that subsidy on 30 June 2026 [13,14,15]. AST describes the award as “up to 148 billion Japanese yen or approximately $1 billion” and says it is still in “advanced discussions” with “no assurance that the joint venture will be finalized or that government financing will be secured” [1]. As of 28 Oct 2026, neither company has published a definitive JV agreement, a satellite purchase contract, or a satellite count, and MIC’s page still shows the grant decision (交付決定) as pending [16].

Question

Short answer

Confidence

How much is the deal worth?

Up to ¥148bn (≈$0.91–1.0bn, depending on FX) of government subsidy, set as a ceiling at 50% of eligible costs [17]. AST calls it “up to approximately $1 billion in non-dilutive, non-debt government capital” [2]. If the full subsidy is used, eligible project costs would be at least ¥296bn (≈$1.8–2.0bn), with the other half from the private side. That figure is an inference that press and analysts draw from the 50% cap, not a disclosed budget [40]. How much revenue flows to AST is not disclosed.

Subsidy ceiling: Confirmed. Total programme size and AST revenue: Unknown.

How many satellites does Japan get?

No official number. On 4 Sep 2026 Japan filed an ITU network called “J-BLUEBIRD-NGSO” with 136 satellites (34 planes × 4, 670 km, 43°). Toyo Keizai links it to RAST, but Rakuten declined to comment [39]. Toyo Keizai had earlier estimated that about 100–130 satellites would be needed for uniform nationwide service [38]. AST says the Japan-flagged satellites are identical BlueBirds that can also be used globally [10]. Initial Rakuten service (targeted for Q4 2026) runs on AST’s shared global constellation, not on dedicated satellites [11,22].

Reported or estimated only.

How much control does Japan get?

The J-LEO rules require the subsidy recipient to own, operate and manage the LEO infrastructure. They also require that all ground facilities serving Japanese users (gateways, satellite control (SOC), payload control (POC) and network control (NOC)) be located in Japan, and that spectrum be coordinated at the ITU through MIC [17]. MIC says RAST was selected because it holds the rights to own and operate the satellites and services [15]. Rakuten leads the JV with roughly equal equity [28,42]. Still unclear: how command authority works when the Japan-flagged satellites fly outside Japan as part of AST’s network, what AST’s TT&C role is, and any lawful-intercept or security terms.

Rules: Confirmed. How RAST applies them: Unknown.

Correction to the premise: The ~$1B figure comes from official sources (AST’s 8-K and Q2 release, plus the CIAJ guidelines), so it is not just an analyst estimate. But it is the maximum government grant, not a contract value, and not money paid by Rakuten. It is also not yet a final award: AST’s own words are “preliminary selection” and “pending government approvals and final agreements” [1,2,10]. The ¥148bn (CIAJ grant cap) and ¥150bn (MIC FY2025 supplementary budget line) are both cited in the press. Dollar conversions vary: Reuters gives $912M, Light Reading $922M and Nikkei $926M [18,30,33,34].

2. What exactly was agreed

2.1 Parties and structure

  • RAST Co., Ltd. (RAST株式会社): the J-LEO application lead. It is the Rakuten–AST joint venture, and its name reflects Rakuten + AST [13,14,39]. Rakuten Mobile, Inc. is the joint proposer [13]. AST’s 8-K calls RAST the “indirect subsidy recipient” [1].
  • Equity split: Mikitani told Nikkei (23 Jun 2026) that the stakes would be “almost equal” (ほぼ対等), with Rakuten Group taking the lead. He did not disclose the investment size and said it “won’t be substantial” [28,42]. No SEC filing shows the JV terms. AST has filed no Item 1.01 (material definitive agreement) 8-K for the JV through 28 Oct 2026; its filings after June are a 7.01 disclosure on 15 Jul 2026 and Item 5.02 governance 8-Ks [1].
  • Government involvement: The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC, 総務省) funded J-LEO from the FY2025 supplementary budget (¥150.0bn) through the Digital Infrastructure Development Fund [18]. The fund is administered by the Communications and Information Network Association of Japan (CIAJ) as fund-holding body [16,17]. The subsidy is a grant (助成), capped at ¥148bn over three fiscal years, at up to 50% of eligible pre-tax costs. Eligible costs include satellites, satellite and ground antenna components, ground facilities, launch services, launch insurance and initial satellite testing [17,40]. Only one winner was to be selected [17].
  • JAXA: JAXA is not a party to J-LEO. Separately, in Feb 2026 Rakuten Mobile’s proposal on AI-driven dynamic spectrum sharing between satellite and terrestrial networks was selected under the JAXA Space Strategy Fund. The theme has up to ¥11bn of total support and runs from Mar 2026 to Mar 2031 [27]. That is an R&D grant, not constellation funding.
  • Spectrum: Rakuten’s 700 MHz band, 715–718 MHz up and 770–773 MHz down, with a 3 MHz channel. MIC received the Council’s technical conditions on 24 Jun 2026 [19,20,21]. Feeder links use Q/V band (39.5–41/42–42.5 GHz down, 45.5–47/48.2–48.7 GHz up) [20].
  • Prepayment / equity investment by Rakuten into AST tied to this deal: none disclosed. In fact, Rakuten Mobile sold about half of its AST shares in April–May 2026 under a BofA trading plan [8,9].

3. Satellites and coverage

3.1 Two layers: shared global service now, Japan-flagged J-LEO satellites later

Layer 1, commercial service from Q4 2026 (shared). Rakuten’s “Rakuten Saikyo Satellite Service Powered by AST SpaceMobile” is targeted to launch from Q4 2026 on AST’s global constellation [22,24]. On 20 Oct 2026 AST listed Japan among the markets where it targets “initial, intermittent coverage” before year-end. During this phase, service is only available when a satellite is overhead [11,12]. After the BB11–13 launch AST reported 13 in-orbit spacecraft [2]. The operational BlueBirds are Block 1 BB1–5 and Block 2 BB6 and BB8–BB13; BB7 was lost [4]. BB14–16 were at Cape Canaveral in October [43]. AST says about 25 satellites give roughly half-day coverage (a US-context remark), and 45–60 enable continuous service in key markets including Japan [10,4].

Layer 2, J-LEO constellation (Japan-flagged). MIC’s schedule runs from the grant decision in FY2026, through procurement, launch and ground build, to D2C service start in FY2028 (by end-Mar 2029), with continued build-out after that [15]. AST’s CEO said on the Q2 call that “the satellites flagged Japanese are basically identical than the rest of the constellation” and that “as they are flagged as Japanese satellites, they can be used anywhere in the world, using the same architecture of gateways and the rest of the American constellation” [10]. So Japan does not get a separate satellite design. It would get a subset of Block 2-class BlueBirds registered or filed under Japan, which also join AST’s global network when they are not over Japan.

3.3 Satellites over Japan at any given time

Not disclosed. The only official parameters are in MIC’s 700 MHz study: a service-link beam diameter of about 48 km, and up to 4 satellites transmitting simultaneously into one area (used for the interference analysis) [20,21]. J-LEO sets the performance target as video-call-capable service about 70% of each day nationwide (ITmedia/Toyo Keizai: 16+ hours), rather than a fixed number of satellites in view [17,36,38]. ITmedia notes that AST’s March 2026 re-filing moved its main shell to 53°, which allows overhead passes across all of Japan including Hokkaido. A new 520 km layer could add capacity over dense areas [37].

3.4 Satellite generation and launch timing

  • Block 1 (BB1–BB5): launched 12 Sep 2024. Used for the April 2025 Japan video call via the Fukushima gateway [24,5].
  • Block 2: BB6 (launched 23 Dec 2025), BB7 (lost 19 Apr 2026), BB8–10 (17 Jun 2026) and BB11–13 (5 Aug 2026). Each has a phased array of about 2,400 sq ft and up to 10× Block 1 bandwidth. Production is through BB50 [4,11].
  • Which FM numbers are Japan-flagged: not disclosed. AST is adding compute capability from BB47–48, and mid-band array production starts later in 2026 [10]. Neither has been linked to J-LEO.
  • Launch risk: New Glenn’s May 2026 pad explosion and the BB7 under-performance. AST says it has 10 launches booked with two providers [10,37,43].

4. Satellite control and sovereignty

J-LEO is designed around 自律性 (autonomy): Japan wants D2C service that cannot be changed or withdrawn by a foreign operator’s decisions. That is why it imposes ownership and domestic-ground-segment conditions that Starlink-based services in Japan do not have [17,36].

Control dimension

Confirmed

Unclear / not public

Ownership of satellites

Recipient must own, operate and manage the LEO infrastructure [17]. MIC: RAST holds the rights to own and operate the satellites and communications services [15]. Rakuten: “Holding the rights to own and operate satellites” [22].

Whether title passes per satellite. Whether AST keeps any lien or step-in rights. Treatment of satellites when used outside Japan [10].

Operator / JV governance

Near-equal JV with Rakuten leading (reported) [28,42].

Board composition, veto rights, deadlock provisions, and AST’s operating role.

TT&C and satellite operations (SOC)

SOC must be located in Japan [17]. Toyo Keizai and ITmedia: satellite control has to be performed from Japan [36,38].

Whether AST’s US operations keep TT&C for Japan-flagged satellites outside Japanese visibility. AST’s US TT&C authority comes from the FCC [5].

Payload control (POC) and network control (NOC)

Must be located in Japan [17].

Who staffs them (RAST or AST contractors). The application had to state the operators’ number, authority and chain of command [17].

Gateways

All gateways serving domestic users must be in Japan [17]. Rakuten already operates a gateway earth station in Fukushima [24]. The 2020 agreement included AST capital for Japanese ground assets [7].

How many gateways RAST will build, and where.

Network core and data

Service runs on Rakuten Mobile’s network. AST says its architecture lets nations keep “all the data and all the management of the infrastructure on the ground” [10].

Explicit data-localisation clauses in the JV or grant.

Lawful intercept / national security

The application had to cover security, cyber-security and supply-chain risk [17].

No deal-specific lawful-intercept, security-clearance or foreign-ownership terms are public. As a licensed carrier, Rakuten Mobile is in any case subject to Japanese telecom law (general context, not deal-specific).

Spectrum rights

Rakuten’s 700 MHz assignment (715–718 / 770–773 MHz), on a non-protection basis. ITU coordination via MIC [17,20]. Japan filed the J-BLUEBIRD network (reported) [39].

Whether AST may use Japan-filed feeder or other rights abroad. Interplay with AST’s own S-band priority rights [11].

Exclusivity in Japan

Rakuten’s 2020 contractual exclusivity for AST capacity in Japan [7].

Whether the J-LEO network will be wholesaled to other MNOs beyond free disaster roaming [17].

Emergency / public-service obligations

Free disaster roaming for partner MNOs. Infrastructure maintained for 5 years after build-out [17].

SLA levels and penalties beyond the grant conditions.

Assessment: On paper, Japan gets a high degree of ground-segment sovereignty and legal ownership: Japanese entity, domestic SOC, POC, NOC and gateways, Japanese ITU filing and Japanese spectrum. The space segment is less sovereign. The satellites are AST-designed and AST-built in Texas, launched by US providers, and deliberately interoperable with AST’s global fleet. Rakuten’s technical dependence on AST for software, upgrades and replacement satellites will continue. J-LEO acknowledges this by requiring only a *study* of domestic manufacturing and launch [17].

5. Context

5.1 Rakuten’s equity stake and relationship with AST

  • 2020: Rakuten co-led AST & Science’s $110M Series B alongside Vodafone and signed a strategic partnership [25,26]. It also signed the Rakuten Agreement covering Japanese exclusivity, a $0.5M/yr fee, AST’s $5M ground investment, KPIs and a $10M penalty that AST accrued in 2023 [7].
  • Shareholding: Rakuten Mobile held 28,520,155 Class A shares after the Oct 2024 restructuring [5]. That fell to 26,080,155 (8.9%) on 16 Apr 2026 [8], then to 15,510,078 (5.3%) when the BofA plan (up to 15,510,077 shares, described as about half its holding) was completed on 5 May 2026. The sales reported for 27 Apr–5 May were at average prices of about $65–76 per share [8,9]. The 2026 proxy, based on an intermediate amendment, showed 21,020,155 (7.0%) [6]. Light Reading reported about 15% in April 2025 [35].
  • Board: Mikitani resigned from AST’s board on 13 Jan 2026. Rakuten no longer meets the threshold to designate a director [6].
  • Commercial: AST recognised $5.7M of gateway equipment sales to Rakuten Mobile in 2025 [6].

How Japan compares: J-LEO carries the largest headline figure attached to any AST partnership, about 5.7× stc’s $175M prepayment. 6. Risks and open questions

  • Finality: Neither the grant decision nor the definitive JV has been published. AST explicitly warns that the JV may not be finalised and that government funding may not be secured [1,16].
  • Private co-funding: At 50% cofunding, RAST needs roughly another ¥148bn if the full subsidy is used. Mikitani says Rakuten’s outlay “won’t be substantial” [42]. How the balance is financed (AST in-kind, debt, or partners) is not disclosed.
  • Schedule: J-LEO requires nationwide service by end-Mar 2029 with video about 70% of the day [17]. AST’s own fleet has slipped: the 45–60 satellite target moved from 2026 to early 2027, BB7 was lost, New Glenn is grounded, and one consultant expects 60 satellites only in 2028 [5,10,43].
  • Spectrum capacity: Only 3+3 MHz at 700 MHz, on a secondary, non-protection basis. Use must not conflict with Rakuten’s approved terrestrial deployment plan [20]. That limits capacity per beam for broadband and video.
  • Dual-use tension: AST wants Japan-flagged satellites to serve globally [10], while Japan wants priority and stability for domestic service [22]. Priority rules, revenue sharing and command authority outside Japan are not public.
  • Rakuten’s commitment signals: Rakuten halved its AST stake in Apr–May 2026 and gave up its board seat [6,8,9]. It may be positioning capital for the JV, but that is not disclosed.
  • Satellite count uncertainty: The 136-satellite ITU filing is a coordination filing, not a procurement order [39]. The number Japan actually buys could be lower.
  • Clawback and long-tail obligations: These include repayment if conditions are breached, five years of post-build service levels, and annual reporting [17].
  • Competitive gap: Three Starlink-based rivals already have millions of users [34,44,45,46]. Rakuten’s differentiation depends on AST delivering broadband and video at scale.
  • Launch dependency: Analysts flag the risk of reliance on SpaceX for launches while competing with Starlink D2C [43].

Open questions to watch: the CIAJ grant decision and amount; an AST 8-K (Item 1.01) or Rakuten release with JV terms; the RAST shareholding; satellite order quantity and FM numbers; location of SOC/NOC sites; wholesale access for other MNOs; and AST’s Q3 2026 results (expected November 2026).

7. Method and source notes

All figures come from the sources cited. Where a number is our own arithmetic it is labelled as such. The earnings-call quotes come from a third-party machine transcript [10]. They are consistent with AST’s filed press release and presentation [2,3], but small transcription errors are possible. Each reference link was checked on 28 Oct 2026 with an automated HTTP request. Links marked [blocked to automated check] returned HTTP 403 to the checker but are official press-release pages that load normally in a browser, so they are kept; a mirror is given where available. Links marked [paywall] resolve, but the full text needs a subscription. Only the headline and lead were used.
